sectionsContent.title: Why Periodic Trends Change
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can explain periodic trends using protons, energy levels, and shielding.

notes.answer: A period is a row. A group is a column.

notes.prompt: Across a row, atoms gain more
notes.answer: protons
They are usually pulled inward.
Li: 3 protons   F: 9 protons

notes.prompt: Down a column, atoms gain another
notes.answer: energy level
Li: 2 levels   Na: 3 levels
Inner electrons reduce the pull felt by outer electrons.

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
Use the checklist to find what still needs practice.
rows.prompt: Explain what changes across a row and what changes down a group, and how each one affects the outer electrons.
rows.answer: Across a row, atoms gain protons, so the outer electrons are pulled inward more. Down a group, atoms gain energy levels, and inner electrons shield the outer ones from the nucleus.
selfCheck: I can tell a period from a group.
I can explain what changes across a row and down a group.

sectionsContent.title: Ionization Energy & Electronegativity
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can describe and explain the trends in ionization energy and electronegativity.

notes.answer: Energy needed to remove an electron from a gas atom.
kJ/mol
Generally increases across a row → and up a column ↑.
More nuclear pull = harder to remove. More distance and shielding = easier.
Br
Same row (period 4). Br has 15 more protons pulling on electrons in the same main energy level.

rows.title: Successive ionization energy
cues: Slide 4: removing electrons one at a time

notes.answer: an inner electron was removed

rows.title: Electronegativity

notes.answer: How strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons in a bond.
No units
Generally increases across a row → and up a column ↑. Fluorine is highest.
More nuclear pull attracts shared electrons. More distance and shielding weaken it.

notes: *Noble gases are not included in this trend.

notes.answer: S < O < F
O is above S. F is right of O.

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
Use the checklist to find what still needs practice.
rows.prompt: Describe the trends in ionization energy and electronegativity, and give the reason for both.
rows.answer: Both generally increase across a row and up a column. More nuclear pull holds electrons tighter; more distance and shielding weaken the pull.
selfCheck: I can define ionization energy and electronegativity.
I can find the valence electrons from a jump in successive ionization energies.
I can rank elements by ionization energy or electronegativity.

sectionsContent.title: Atomic & Ionic Radius
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can describe and explain the atomic radius trend and compare an ion to its atom.

notes.answer: The size of an atom.
picometers (pm)
Generally increases down a column ↓ and to the left across a row ←.
Down: another energy level adds size. Across: more protons pull electrons inward.
Ca
Both are in period 4. Br has more protons pulling its electrons inward.

rows.title: Ion size: magnesium
cues: Slide 7: magnesium loses its two outer electrons

notes.answer: The outer level is gone. The nucleus still has 12 protons.

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
Use the checklist to find what still needs practice.
rows.prompt: Describe the atomic radius trend, give both reasons, and explain why the magnesium ion is smaller than the magnesium atom.
rows.answer: Radius increases down a column (another energy level) and to the left across a row (fewer protons pulling inward). The magnesium ion lost its outer level, and the same 12 protons hold fewer electrons.
selfCheck: I can define atomic radius and give its units.
I can compare the sizes of two atoms in the same period or group.
I can explain why a positive ion is smaller than its atom.

sectionsContent.title: Melting & Boiling Points; Trend Summary
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can describe the melting and boiling point patterns in groups 1 and 17 and summarize the periodic trends.

notes.answer: solid → liquid
liquid → gas
°C
No single trend across the whole table. Down group 1: both fall (Li → Cs). Down group 17: both rise (F → I).
Stronger attractions usually need more energy to overcome. Different bonds give different patterns.
Iodine, I₂
Larger halogen molecules attract each other more strongly.

rows.title: Trend summary
cues: Slide 9: the two corners of the table

rows: Larger atomic radius, stronger metallic character

notes.answer: How easily an atom loses electrons; strong near Cs.

notes: *Use the arrows to label your Gizmo sheet. There are exceptions.

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
Use the checklist to find what still needs practice.
rows.prompt: Summarize which way each trend points, and explain why melting and boiling points have no single trend.
rows.answer: Ionization energy and electronegativity rise toward the top right; atomic radius and metallic character rise toward the bottom left. Melting and boiling points depend on the attractions in each group: they fall down group 1 and rise down group 17.
selfCheck: I can define melting point, boiling point, and metallic character.
I can describe the melting and boiling point patterns in groups 1 and 17.
I can state which corner of the table each trend points to.

conceptReview.title: Concept Review
conceptReview.subtitle: Periodic trends, from the unit slides

sections.heading: Why trends change
paragraphs: **Across a row:** more protons pull the outer electrons inward.
**Down a group:** another energy level; inner electrons shield the outer ones.
sections.watchOut: Shielding comes from inner electrons, not from protons.

sections.heading: Ionization energy and electronegativity
paragraphs: **Ionization energy:** energy to remove an electron (kJ/mol). **Electronegativity:** pull on shared electrons (no units).
Both generally increase across a row and up a column. A large jump in successive ionization energies marks the first inner electron.
sections.watchOut: Noble gases are left out of the electronegativity trend.

sections.heading: Atomic and ionic radius
paragraphs: **Atomic radius:** the size of an atom, in pm. Increases down a column and to the left across a row.
**The magnesium ion is smaller than the atom:** its outer level is gone, and the same 12 protons hold fewer electrons.
sections.watchOut: Radius runs opposite to ionization energy and electronegativity.

sections.heading: Melting and boiling points
paragraphs: No single trend across the table. Down group 1 both fall; down group 17 both rise.
**Toward the top right:** higher IE and EN. **Toward the bottom left:** larger radius, stronger metallic character.
sections.watchOut: Melting and boiling points are temperatures (°C), not energies.
